hook: Socrates' pupil, who founded the Academy and wrote philosophy's most famous books.

pages.t: A wrestler from a noble family
pages.x: Plato was born around 428 BC into one of the leading families of Athens. An old story says "Plato", meaning "broad", was a wrestling nickname for his wide shoulders. He hoped to go into politics, until he met Socrates and the trial and death of his teacher turned him against the politics of Athens.

Plato travelled to Italy, where he met followers of Pythagoras, and to Syracuse in Sicily, where he tried to turn its tyrant, Dionysius, into a wise ruler. The story goes that the tyrant grew so annoyed that he had Plato sold as a slave, until a friend bought his freedom. He went back to Syracuse twice more, and failed both times.

Around 387 BC he set up a school in a grove outside Athens named after the hero Akademos. Often called the first university in Europe, it taught philosophy, mathematics and astronomy for some three centuries. A later story says the door bore the words: "Let no one ignorant of geometry enter."

Plato wrote dialogues, plays of ideas with Socrates as the hero. The most famous, The Republic, asks what justice is and imagines a perfect state ruled by philosopher kings. All his dialogues survive, about 35 of them, a rare piece of luck for an ancient writer.

In The Republic, Plato imagines prisoners chained in a cave, who see only shadows on the wall and think they are real. One escapes into the sunlight and sees the real world. When he goes back to tell the others, they laugh at him. It is his picture of how learning frees the mind.

Plato's dialogues are the foundation of Western philosophy; one modern thinker said all of it is "a series of footnotes to Plato". His ideas about justice, love, the soul and a perfect world beyond this one shaped Christian and Islamic thought.
